lines: An order service finishes committing its own order to its own database, right before it was supposed to tell anyone else about it.
The step that was supposed to announce the order never actually runs, because the service crashes at exactly that moment.
The warehouse never learns the order exists at all, and the only place that order lives from now on is inside that one database.
Before I show you what actually happened to that order, think through this with me.
Committing the order succeeded completely. The separate step meant to tell anyone else about it never got the chance to run at all.
Is that missing announcement something the system can still recover somehow, or is it simply gone for good?
answer: The database only ever recorded that an order exists. It never recorded that telling anyone else about it was still owed.
It's gone completely, because nothing anywhere ever wrote down that a second step was supposed to follow the first one.

lines: Here's the fix underneath everything this lesson is actually about.
Instead of announcing a change as a separate step afterward, a service writes that announcement into its own database, in the exact same transaction as the change itself.
From that point forward, something reading the database's own log, not the application, is the one responsible for actually sending that announcement onward.
I confirmed both halves of that directly, against this sandbox's own real database.
Committing an order and then crashing before a separate announcement step left nothing at all behind for a decoding read to find.

Writing that same announcement into the database as part of the order's own transaction meant a decoding read could always find it, every single time, because the two writes were never actually separate.
Here's what the piece that reads this announcement table actually does with each row.
It names a destination for each row based on what kind of aggregate the row is about, and it treats that row's own unique identifier as a way for a downstream reader to avoid double-counting it.
If somebody later deletes a row from this same announcement table, that deletion itself never gets forwarded as a fake announcement.
I measured that routing and that deduplication directly, against two real rows decoded from this sandbox's own database.
One row, about an order, landed at one destination, while a second row, about a shipment, landed at a completely different one.
Each of those two rows still carried its own unique identifier along with it, ready for whatever reads it downstream to use for deduplication.
Now here's something worth confirming about order, since several aggregates can share the same announcement table at once.
I wrote four rows for two completely different aggregates, deliberately interleaving them rather than writing each aggregate's own rows together.
Once I separated them back out by which aggregate each row actually belonged to, each one's own sequence came out in exactly the order it was actually written.
Here's the part of today's lesson that decides whether a routine bit of table maintenance is ever actually dangerous.
I let the decoding read capture a row first, and only afterward did I delete that same row from the announcement table.
That later deletion produced no announcement at all, confirming that maintenance is both invisible downstream and already safe once a row has already been captured.
Let's put together everything today's lesson actually showed, because four separate pieces all lean on one idea.
Writing an announcement as part of the original transaction, rather than as a separate step, turns a risky second act into a single guaranteed one.

Routing, deduplication and staying correctly ordered are each a direct consequence of that one same guarantee, and routine table maintenance only stays safe because of exactly that same guarantee too.
One more question, because a team might assume filtering out stray deletions covers every risk by itself.
Say a team deletes old rows from this announcement table the moment they're written, without ever confirming a decoding read already captured them.
Is that kind of immediate table maintenance still safe to run?
answer: Filtering a deletion out only stops that deletion itself from being forwarded as a fake announcement to begin with.
It does nothing at all to protect a row that gets removed before a decoding read ever got the chance to see the insert that actually mattered.
